Saturday, 7 February 2037. Elena has come back to Berlin for a week. The envelope with the results from the Goethe-Institut has arrived at Lena's address. Everyone is in the café.
Here you are. The envelope we've been waiting for for three months.
I can't open it. My hands are shaking like Grete's.
Then I'll open it. After all, I'm the teacher whose pupil you are.
Slowly, Elif. Like a cup of coffee.
“Goethe-Zertifikat B2. Result: passed.” Reading: ninety per cent. Listening: eighty-eight. Writing: eighty-six. Speaking: ninety-four!
Because of your accent. I always said it was charming.
And writing, the module you were most afraid of: eighty-six!
I owe that to a journalist with a red pen and a girl who taught me “Mit freundlichen Grüßen”.
And to the cake. Don't forget the cake.
The practical rule: if the article already shows gender and case (der, dem, des), the adjective takes -e or -en. If it doesn't (ein, no article), the adjective shows the gender itself (-er, -es).
In speech, “wegen” and “trotz” often appear with the dative too (wegen dem Wetter), but in the exam use the genitive.

After “alles, etwas, nichts, das Beste” you use “was”, not “das”: “Das ist alles, was ich weiß.”

The envelope from the Goethe-Institut came on a grey Tuesday at the beginning of February two thousand and thirty-seven, to Lena and Andrei's address, because Elena had given it when she registered, “so that I don't have to open it alone”. Lena put it unopened on the shelf behind the counter, next to the brass bell, and rang Elena in Sibiu. Elena said she would come. She came on Friday, on the night train, eighteen hours, for an envelope, as Dan remarked on the phone, “that you could just as well have photographed with your phone”. But Elena didn't want to see it photographed. She wanted to hold it in her hand, in the café, under the bell, with the people without whom, as she said, “there would only be numbers in this envelope”.

On Saturday afternoon the café was full. Not as full as at Ludwig's reading, but full enough for Lena to hang a sign on the door: “Heute geschlossene Gesellschaft. Klingeln trotzdem erlaubt.” (Private event today. Ringing still allowed.) Everyone who had helped during the ten autumn weeks was there. Elif, with Leo's old stopwatch in her pocket, out of habit. Katrin Krüger, with her red pen, also out of habit. Ludwig, at his table by the window. Hotte, who since his ninety-second birthday two weeks before had been claiming that he was “now officially the oldest on Kastanienallee, and that comes with obligations”. Dr Vogt, who had sacrificed his day off. Leo and Abena, both in BVG uniform, straight from the morning shift. And Yusuf, who had come from Neukölln, with a bunch of tulips and the news that he had passed too, with eighty-three per cent, “less than you, because of the donkeys”.

Yusuf had another piece of news. He told Elena quietly, to one side, while the others were sharing out cake. His mother in Aleppo had started learning German in December, at sixty, on an online course, in the evenings, at the kitchen table, with the slip of paper on the fridge: “Not every note. The melody.” She had found a teacher, a student from Damascus, twenty-two years old, “younger than her grandchildren”, Yusuf said and laughed. Last week she had sent him a message in German for the first time, four words, with two mistakes: “Ich lerne. Bald komme.” He showed Elena his phone. Elena read the four words and then took out of her bag her twelfth notebook, the secret one, and wrote them in it, under the twenty-three Berlin words, with the two mistakes, without correcting them.

Elif opened the envelope, because Elena's hands were shaking too much, and she opened it slowly, as Ludwig had told her, like a cup of coffee filled to the brim. Inside there was a single sheet, with the blue Goethe-Institut logo, and Elif read it aloud, the most important thing first: “Result: passed.” Then the numbers, module by module. With each number the café got noisier. Ninety in reading, and Elif looked proudly over at Katrin. Eighty-eight in listening, and Dr Vogt nodded contentedly, as if he had taken the exam himself. Eighty-six in writing, and Katrin Krüger put down her red pen for the first time that day. And ninety-four in speaking, and Ludwig said, loudly enough for everyone to hear: “Because of the accent. I always said so.”

Elena said nothing for a long time. She took the sheet, read it herself, line by line, slowly, and this time she read every word, because, as she explained later, it was the only time it was worth it. Then she got up, went to the brass bell, took off the felt, although it was Saturday and Dr Vogt wasn't asleep anyway but sitting at a table, and rang. Once. Loudly. With the cord, not with her finger. And then, after a moment, once more. “The second time”, she said, in German, into the silence, “is for Grete. Without whom I'd never have found the melody.” Nobody said anything. Hotte took off his cap. And Elif looked out of the window, into the courtyard, at the bare chestnut tree, under which the urn was to be buried in April, and whispered something nobody understood except Ludwig, who was sitting next to her: “Do you hear? She rang.”

Then Elena called Dan, on video, and held the sheet up to the camera, and Dan, in his kitchen in Sibiu, with the old German exercise book in front of him, put on his glasses and read, slowly, moving his lips. He didn't understand everything. But he understood “bestanden”, and he understood the numbers, and then he did something Elena had seen only twice in thirty-five years of marriage: he cried. Not much. Just a little. Then he wiped his eyes with the back of his hand, cleared his throat and said, in German, with the worst accent ever heard in Berlin: “Ich bin stolz. Ich bin der Mann von Elena. Sie spricht Deutsch.” It was, as Elif worked out later, the longest German utterance Dan had ever made. Three sentences. Eleven words. Page six of his exercise book.

The following week Katrin Krüger wrote a short article for the local page, with the headline “Die Frau, die nicht mehr jedes Wort liest” (The woman who no longer reads every word). She wrote about a beekeeper's wife from Transylvania, fifty-eight years old, who had studied alone for five years at the kitchen table and then for ten weeks in Berlin, with a twelve-year-old teacher, a retired tram driver, an anaesthetist and a hundred-year-old pianist, “whose advice still goes with her today”. Elena read the article in Sibiu, at the kitchen table, printed out by Dan, and rang Katrin to thank her. “You made a mistake”, she said, in German, very seriously. “In the third paragraph. «Trotz ihrem Akzent». You say «trotz ihres Akzents». With the genitive.” At the other end there was a long silence. Then Katrin laughed so loudly that Elena had to hold the phone away from her ear.

It could have been the loveliest moment of the afternoon. But then Leo stood up. He had sat quietly in the corner all afternoon, next to Abena, fiddling with his old white cup, the cup with the BVB logo, which he had taken everywhere since the exam. Now he put it on the table, very carefully, and cleared his throat, and everyone looked at him, because Leo never cleared his throat. He was, as his mother said, a Brandt of the quiet sort. “I want to say something too”, he said. “I know today is Elena's day. But Abena said that if I don't say it today, I'll never say it.” Abena, beside him, nodded seriously. Leo took a deep breath. “Abena and I”, he said, “have got engaged. Yesterday. In the cab of the M10, at the Warschauer Straße terminus, at twelve minutes past two, during the turnaround break.”

The café went so quiet that you could hear the coffee machine, which Lena had forgotten to switch off. Then everyone jumped up at once. Elif screamed. Hotte banged his walking stick on the floor so hard that the glasses rattled. Ludwig got up, slowly, leaning on his stick, went over to Leo and hugged him, for a long time, without saying anything, then hugged Abena, and then said, in a voice that wasn't quite steady: “In the cab. Of course in the cab. Where else.” Abena laughed. She told them that Leo had hidden the ring in the old white cup, under a napkin, and had handed her the cup with the words: “Carry it without spilling anything.” And that she had almost dropped the cup when she saw the ring. “Almost”, said Leo. “But not quite. She's the better tram driver of the two of us. One point zero.”

Hotte had sat down again in the meantime, breathing heavily from getting up, and was looking at Leo and Abena over the rim of his glass. “I've got two conditions”, he announced. “One: the wedding's in summer, not winter. I'm ninety-two, I get cold. Two: you go there in the Tatra. Like Lena.” Leo looked at Kurt Wolff's seat, which was empty that afternoon, and then at Ludwig. Ludwig nodded. “I'll talk to Kurt”, he said. “But this time the bride drives.” Abena laughed and said she had never driven a Tatra. “Then you'll learn”, said Ludwig. “I'll teach you. How to start it.” And everyone knew, without anyone saying it, what that meant: that Ludwig would need the white cup one more time.

At that moment Lena went behind the counter, opened the bottom drawer, in which, as everyone knew, she kept the things she didn't want to lose, and took out a hatbox. Inside, wrapped in tissue paper, was the little black hat with the feather. Grete's hat. Which she had left to Lena “for the next wedding, which is sure to come, I know it, she doesn't know it yet”. Lena had wondered at the time which wedding she meant. Now she knew. She went over to Abena and gave her the box. “It's from a woman you barely knew”, she said. “But she knew you. She knew, in the summer. Before you two did.” Abena opened the box and looked at the hat for a long time. Then she put it on, carefully, on her dark curls, and it fitted as if it had been made for her.

“How did she know?” Leo asked quietly, later, when most of the guests had gone and only the family was still sitting in the café. Ludwig thought about it. Then he told them about a Wednesday in July, shortly after Leo's oral exam, when Leo and Abena had come to the care home together to tell Grete their marks, one point three and one point zero, and how they had sat side by side at Grete's bed, both in uniform, and how Abena, without realising it, had held Leo's hand the whole time. “Grete didn't say anything”, said Ludwig. “She just looked at the hands. And afterwards, when you'd gone, she said to me: those two are on the same line. They just don't know it yet.” Leo looked at his hand, in which Abena's hand lay, as in July, without either of them having noticed.

Later in the evening Abena called her parents in Kumasi, on video, from the table by the window, and held the phone so that everyone in the café could be seen. Her mother cried, her father asked Leo a long question in Twi, which Abena wouldn't translate, and Leo, who had been practising secretly for weeks, answered with the only three words of Twi he knew: “Medaase. Me dɔ wo.” Thank you. I love you. Abena's father gave him a long look. Then he laughed, a deep, loud laugh, and said something that this time Abena did translate: “He says you speak Twi like a tram driver.” Ludwig, at the next table, choked on his coffee. “That's the greatest compliment”, he said, when he had got his breath back, “you can get in this family.”

In the evening, as Elena was packing for Sunday's night train, Elif came up to the first floor once more, with a little parcel. It was a notebook. A new notebook, the thirteenth, with a blue cover, and on the first page Elif had written, in her round, neat handwriting: “Für C1. Ab jetzt nicht mehr jedes Wort. Nur die wichtigen.” (For C1. From now on, not every word any more. Only the important ones.) Elena laughed. “C1?” she asked. “I'm fifty-eight.” Elif shrugged. “Grete was a hundred and was still learning how to let go”, she said. “You've got time.” Elena took the notebook and held it in her hands for a while. Then she wrote the first word in it, without looking it up in the dictionary, without hesitating: “Weitermachen.” And underneath, smaller, in Romanian: “Mulțumesc, profesoară.” (“Thank you, teacher.”)
